about: Sourced life stories for the prophets of Jeremiah's day (Zephaniah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Obadiah) and the four prophets Jeremiah opposed. Written from Scripture and the dossier Research/People/prophets-jeremiah.md. Jeremiah's own story is in another file.

zephaniah-zep-1-1.short: Zephaniah son of Cushi received the word of the LORD in the days of Josiah king of Judah, and proclaimed the day of the LORD.

paragraphs.text: All that Scripture tells of Zephaniah himself is in the first verse of his book. The word of the LORD came to him “in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah”. He is named as the son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hizkiah. Scripture tells nothing more of his life.

His book warns that “the great day of the LORD is near”, a day of wrath on Judah and Jerusalem, on those who worshipped Baal and the host of heaven, and on the nations around: the Philistines, Moab and Ammon, the Ethiopians, and Assyria with its city Nineveh.

He calls the meek of the earth to seek the LORD, and near the end of his book calls the daughter of Zion to sing. The LORD would leave “an afflicted and poor people” who trust in his name, and would rejoice over Zion “with singing”.

nahum-nam-1-1.short: Nahum the Elkoshite saw the vision of the fall of Nineveh, and brought Judah word that the oppressor would be cut off.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names him only as “Nahum the Elkoshite”, in the first line of his book, which is “The burden of Nineveh”. It gives no father, no king and no story of his life.
His book speaks of the LORD as “slow to anger, and great in power”, a strong hold for those who trust in him, who takes vengeance on his enemies.

To Judah he brought comfort: “Behold upon the mountains the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace!” Its yoke would be broken. To Nineveh, “the bloody city”, he foretold siege and ruin, and reminded it of “populous No”, which for all its strength had gone “into captivity”.

habakkuk-hab-1-1.short: Habakkuk the prophet asked the LORD how long wrong would go unpunished, waited for the answer, and ended his book in a song of trust.

paragraphs.text: Scripture calls him “Habakkuk the prophet” and tells nothing of his family, his home or his king. What it gives is his book, which begins with his own cry: “O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!”

The LORD answered that he was raising up the Chaldeans, “that bitter and hasty nation”. Habakkuk asked again how the LORD could look on while the wicked devoured the man more righteous than he, and said he would stand upon his watch to see what answer would come.

He was told to write the vision plainly and to wait for it: “the just shall live by his faith”. The New Testament quotes these words three times. Woes follow on the one who builds by violence and on the maker of idols, and then: “let all the earth keep silence before him.”

His last chapter is a prayer set for music. He trembled at what he heard, yet said that though the fig tree should not blossom and the flock be cut off, “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.”

obadiah-oba-1-1.short: Obadiah's vision, a book of twenty-one verses, speaks against Edom for its violence against its brother Jacob.

paragraphs.text: Scripture names him only in the first words of his book, “The vision of Obadiah”. It gives no father, home or king for him.

The vision is against Edom, which trusted in its dwelling “in the clefts of the rock”; the LORD would bring it down. Its fault was that it stood on the other side when strangers entered Jerusalem's gates: “For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee”.
It ends with the day of the LORD on all the nations, “as thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee”, with deliverance on mount Zion, and with the words “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.”

hananiah-jer-28-1.short: Hananiah son of Azur, a prophet of Gibeon, broke Jeremiah's yoke and promised the captives' return within two years; Jeremiah said the LORD had not sent him.

paragraphs.text: Hananiah was the son of Azur, “of Gibeon”. In the fourth year of Zedekiah, in the fifth month, he spoke to Jeremiah in the house of the LORD, before the priests and all the people.

He said in the LORD's name, “I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon,” and that within two full years the temple vessels, King Jeconiah and all the captives would come back from Babylon. Jeremiah answered, “Amen: the LORD do so”, but reminded him that a prophet who prophesies peace is known when his word comes to pass.

Then Hananiah took the yoke from Jeremiah's neck and broke it, saying that so the LORD would break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar. Jeremiah went his way. Afterwards the word came to Jeremiah that the LORD had put a yoke of iron on the nations.

Jeremiah told him, “The LORD hath not sent thee; but thou makest this people to trust in a lie,” and that he would die that year because he had taught rebellion against the LORD. “So Hananiah the prophet died the same year in the seventh month.”

ahab-jer-29-21.short: Ahab son of Kolaiah prophesied among the captives in Babylon; Jeremiah's letter said he prophesied a lie in the LORD's name.

paragraphs.text: Ahab the son of Kolaiah was one of the prophets among the captives in Babylon. Scripture names him only in Jeremiah's letter to the captives, together with Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah.

The letter said the two of them prophesied “a lie unto you in my name”, and charged them with adultery with their neighbours' wives. The LORD would deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar, who would slay them before the captives' eyes.
Their names would become a curse among the captives: “The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”. Scripture records nothing else of him.

zedekiah-jer-29-21.short: Zedekiah son of Maaseiah prophesied among the captives in Babylon; Jeremiah's letter said he prophesied a lie in the LORD's name.

paragraphs.text: Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah was one of the prophets among the captives in Babylon. He is a different man from Zedekiah king of Judah, in whose reign Jeremiah's letter was sent. The letter names him together with Ahab the son of Kolaiah.

The letter said the two of them prophesied “a lie unto you in my name”, and charged them with adultery with their neighbours' wives. The LORD would deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar, who would slay them before the captives' eyes.
Their names would become a curse among the captives: “The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”. Scripture records nothing else of him.

shemaiah-jer-29-24.short: Shemaiah the Nehelamite, among the captives, wrote to Jerusalem asking why Jeremiah had not been reproved; the LORD said, “I sent him not.”

paragraphs.text: Shemaiah the Nehelamite was among the captives in Babylon. When Jeremiah wrote telling them that the captivity would be long, Shemaiah sent letters in his own name to the people at Jerusalem, to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, and to all the priests.

He reminded Zephaniah that he had been made priest to put “every man that is mad, and maketh himself a prophet” in prison and in the stocks, and asked, “why hast thou not reproved Jeremiah of Anathoth”? Zephaniah read the letter in Jeremiah's ears.

Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, to send to all the captives: Shemaiah had prophesied to them though “I sent him not”, and had caused them to trust in a lie. He and his seed would have no man to dwell among the people, and he would not see the good the LORD would do.
